1:
Chrysostom explains why the argument turns to Abraham at just this point. Having said that the world had become guilty, that all had sinned, and that boasting was excluded, the apostle is now intent on showing that a salvation received by faith is so far from being matter of shame that it is the cause of a brighter glory than any through works; and since the Jews kept turning over the fact that the patriarch was the first to receive circumcision, he means to show that Abraham too was justified by faith. Chrysostom notes the method as well as the matter — the discourse is carried forward by question, as this writer always does for clearness' sake. Gill puts the choice of example plainly: the apostle instances in the greatest person of their nation, for whom they had the greatest esteem. Calvin calls it a confirmation by example and a very strong one, since all things are alike in the subject and the person: Abraham was the father of the faithful, and in him was exhibited a mirror and pattern of righteousness belonging to the whole Church, so that his posterity, who claimed a righteousness of their own by the law, ought to have been silenced through shame. Barnes hears the opening words as the objection of a Jew rather than the apostle's own — how does this doctrine agree with what the Scriptures say of Abraham?

Where the phrase according to the flesh attaches is disputed, and the dispute is not idle. Ellicott takes the construction to be settled by position, since in the best manuscripts the words are separated from the verb and joined to the noun, so that they mean simply our father by natural descent. Robertson notes that the manuscripts differ in exactly that placing, and that the word for forefather is an old one occurring only here in the New Testament. Barnes calls the expression much controverted and comes down the other way: the connexion with the verb is doubtless the proper one, so the question is what Abraham found in respect to the flesh. As to what flesh means, he reports that some refer it to external privileges, some to Abraham's own strength, some to circumcision, and takes the last for correct. Calvin surveys the same options and settles differently, thinking the words expressed as a thing peculiar to the Jews — for it was a greater honour to be children of Abraham by descent than by mere adoption, provided there was also faith. He concedes them that closer bond, but only to impress that they ought not to depart from their father's example.

Clarke is in no doubt: the phrase must refer to the sign in Abraham's flesh, his circumcision, on which the Jew would found his right to peculiar blessings. He arranges the whole chapter as a dialogue in which the Jew asks one question, contained in this verse and part of the next, and the apostle's answer takes up all the rest. Wesley reads it as by works, and quotes Theodoret to the same effect, that the phrase means what is of works, inasmuch as it is by our fleshly bodies that works are done. Barnes sets out the plan of what follows: the argument is drawn first from Abraham and then from David, and meets the further question whether the justification was not a consequence of circumcision by showing that Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, the circumcision being a public seal of the fact. Henry, taking the verb rather than the phrase, observes that all the world is seeking, but that while most weary themselves for very vanity none can be reckoned to have found except those justified before God — so Abraham, like a wise merchant seeking goodly pearls, found this one pearl of great price.
2:
The verse is a piece of an argument rather than a whole one, and Calvin says so in the technical term: it is an incomplete argument, an attempted but unfinished process of reasoning, and it is not the character of Scripture, or of any other writing, to discuss matters in the form of a syllogism. The clause before us is the minor proposition, and the conclusion has to be supplied. Wesley supplies it: if Abraham had been justified by works he would have had room to glory; but he had not room to glory; therefore he was not justified by works. Barnes gives the same three steps and credits Calvin with the wording — if Abraham was justified by his works he might boast of his own merits, but he has no ground of boasting before God, therefore he was not justified by works. Gill states the negative side flatly, that Abraham was not and could not be justified by works, and that this is clear from what follows if it were supposed otherwise.

Clarke keeps up the dialogue he began in the previous verse, giving the first clause to the Jew, who concludes that Abraham was justified by obedience to the law of circumcision and so has something to exult in, and the second to the apostle. Allowing, he makes him answer, that Abraham might glory in being called out of heathenish darkness into such marvellous light, and exult in the privileges God had granted him, still that glorying was not before God as a reason why the privileges should be granted — the glorying itself being a consequence of the privileges. Ellicott calls the abruptness an instance of the writer's rapid and eager dialectic: if the whole train of thought had been given it would have run much longer, but the greater part is suppressed and he strikes straight at the one point he means to bring into relief, that whatever there may be before men there is no boasting before God. Robertson adds that the condition is of the first class, assumed as true for the sake of argument though untrue in fact, and recalls that the rabbis had a doctrine of the merits of Abraham, who was held to have a superfluity of credits to pass on to his descendants. Abraham deserved all the respect from men that came to him, Robertson allows, but his relation to God was a different matter.

Calvin dwells on the noun, which is not the word used a chapter earlier but one meaning the reason or ground or cause of glorying — rendered by Grotius as that whereby a man may hope for praise. He reports another reading of the phrase before God, given by Vatablus, which takes it as meaning with regard to what God has said in his word, a view confirmed by the question that immediately follows about what the Scripture says. And he defines the thing denied: glorying is when we pretend to have anything of our own to which a reward is supposed to be due at God's tribunal — so that since it is taken away from Abraham, who of us can claim for himself the least particle of merit? Barnes reaches the same end by the shorter road, that the apostle appeals at once to the Scriptures to show there is no record of any such ground of boasting, and that since God judges right in all cases it follows that Abraham had none. Wesley quotes Theodoret on what is gained by the exchange: the full performance of good works crowns the doers with the prize but does not exhibit the loving-kindness of God, whereas faith sets forth both the disposition of the believer toward God and the loving-kindness of God, who by accepting such faith proclaims the man who has it victorious.
3:
Gill notes that the question is a Jewish formula, used when anything is proposed which seems contrary to Scripture, as justification by works does here. Clarke calls the account in Genesis decisive, and Barnes agrees the inspired record was final; he adds what the faith was about, namely that Abraham's posterity should be as the stars of heaven, a promise made when he had no child and no prospect of any, so that what was reckoned was a strong and unwavering act of confidence. Ellicott observes that the same verse was elaborately commented on by Philo and others, so it seems to have been a common topic in the Jewish schools, and that it stands as a comment on Abraham's belief in the promise of a numerous posterity. Wesley finds a second object behind the first, since besides the promise about his seed there was especially the promise concerning Christ, through whom all nations should be blessed.

What faith means is not quite the same question. Ellicott notices that the word is not used in the same sense in the original and in the application: in Abraham's case it was trust in the fulfilment of a promise, while in this writer's usage it is rather an enthusiastic adhesion to a person — part of a general enlargement of Old Testament terminology, where Hebrews applies the word more strictly and James in a thinner sense still, of merely intellectual assent. Barnes is concerned to keep it from being made into a thing. Faith is always an act of the mind; it is not a created essence placed within the mind, nor a substance put there by almighty power, nor a principle — the expression a principle of faith being as unmeaning as a principle of joy, or of sorrow, or of remorse. God promises, the man believes, and this is the whole of it. Calvin widens the object instead: the word in Genesis is not to be confined to any particular expression but refers to the whole covenant of salvation and the grace of adoption; those who think Moses' testimony has been drawn aside from its obvious meaning have not considered that it extends to the whole context, and have begun in the wrong place, since God gave it to make Abraham more assured of his adoption.

On the word rendered counted the bench divides in earnest. Robertson takes it as an old and common verb for setting down accounts, literally or metaphorically: the believing was set down on the credit side of the ledger. Barnes goes much further, having examined every occurrence of the underlying Hebrew word in the Old Testament and some forty in the New; his conclusion is that there is not one place where it is used of reckoning to a man what does not strictly belong to him, so that no doctrine of transferring, whether of sin or of holiness, can be derived from it — and that what is declared to be reckoned, by Moses and by Paul alike, is the act of believing. Ellicott takes the opposite view plainly: the sense of imputation is not to be got rid of, being distinctly a forensic act, and the righteousness attributed to Abraham is not actual but something else treated as if it were equivalent, by God acting as the judge of men. He notes in passing that our version renders the same words five different ways across the several places where they occur. Calvin takes the same side and gives a reason: if there were any righteousness by works it would have to be in men themselves, whereas by faith they derive from another what is wanting in themselves, so the righteousness of faith is rightly called imputative. Moses, he adds, does not tell us what men thought of Abraham, but how he was accounted before the tribunal of God.
4:
Barnes cautions that the verse does not affirm that anyone has actually worked out salvation by conformity to the law; it states a general principle about works. Where a man fulfils the terms of a contract, paying him is not a matter of favour — he has earned it, and we are bound to pay. So if a man were justified by his works he would have a claim on God, and it would be wrong not to justify him; which Barnes takes as a further reason the doctrine cannot be true. The word for reward, he adds, is the ordinary word for the pay of soldiers and day-labourers, and reckoned here carries its strict and proper sense, to reckon as belonging to a man what is already his own or due to him. Ellicott presses the same point: the relation between what such a man receives and what he does is that of wages for work done, claimable if need be in a court of law, and there is in it no element of grace, or favour, or concession. Robertson notes the phrase is simply not according to grace but according to what is owed. Wesley makes it flat — to him that works all the law requires, the reward is no favour but an absolute debt.

Both Gill and Calvin are anxious that the worker not be misidentified. Gill distinguishes the man who works from principles of grace, regenerate and disposed to work for God, working freely and to a right end, from the worker meant here, who works on nature's principles and with selfish views, trusting to and glorying in what he does and seeking righteousness by his work. Calvin draws the line in the same place: the worker is not the man given to good works, to which all God's children ought to attend, but the man who seeks to merit something by them; and the non-worker is not the idle man but the one who does not depend on the merit of what he does. Paul forbids the faithful to be mercenaries, demanding anything from God as justly their due. Calvin adds that the argument hangs not on a single expression but on the whole passage, and finds the same reasoning in Galatians 3:11, where the law promises reward to works while the just live by faith. Clarke, tracking the vocabulary, observes that the translators render one Greek verb variously through this chapter as counted, reckoned, and imputed, and that reckoned is probably the best sense throughout.

Clarke takes the case as Abraham's own: he was called when he was ungodly, an idolater, and on believing was freely justified; and since all have sinned, justification, if it takes place at all, must take place on behalf of the ungodly. Ellicott notes the word is stronger than merely unrighteous, and belongs to the general form of the proposition rather than to Abraham, since faith and positive impiety would hardly in fact be found together. Barnes works hardest here, and works to keep the language honest. God does not first esteem such men pure, contrary to fact; knowing they are defiled and deserve no favour, he resolves to treat them as friends. The righteousness of Christ is not transferred to them, for moral character cannot be transferred, nor infused into them, for then they could not be spoken of as ungodly; rather the results of Christ's death are so reckoned to believers as to make it proper for God to treat them as righteous in his sight. Wesley draws out the order: this shows how groundless the opinion is that holiness is previous to justification, since a man could not be justified were he not at that very moment ungodly.
6:
Having instanced Abraham, the father of the nation, Paul turns to a second witness, and Gill notes the choice is deliberate: David was a person of great note and esteem among the Jews, and he describes the happiness of justified persons in a very lively manner. Barnes reads the move as an argument from precedent — the doctrine being defended is not new, and not contrary to the Old Testament, and David is shown to have understood the same justification without works. Wesley adds that David is fitly introduced after Abraham because he also received and delivered down the promise, and that without works means without regard to any former good works supposed to have been done by him. Robertson observes that the verb Paul uses is not simply to describe but to pronounce blessing, a rare word for felicitation or congratulation, and Ellicott would render it speaks the felicitation, or pronounces blessed. Barnes takes the whole scope of the psalm to be the blessedness of the man who is forgiven, whose sins are not charged on him: being pardoned, he is treated henceforward as a righteous man and a friend of God.

Calvin uses the citation as a lever against two positions at once. Against those who limit the works of the law to ceremonies, he answers that Paul here says works with nothing added, and a simple unrestricted expression must be understood of every work without difference. Against those who would have satisfaction made for sin, he answers that righteousness is here nothing else than the remission of sins, and that this remission is gratuitous by the very name of it: the creditor who is paid does not remit, but he who spontaneously cancels the debt through mere kindness. He notices too that Paul stops short and does not finish the verse, leaving out the words about the man in whose spirit there is no guile — evidently because his subject is justification and not sanctification, which marks the difference between the two most clearly. And the schoolmen's half remission, where the fault is pardoned while the punishment is retained, cannot stand: how should God punish sins which he does not impute?

The psalm heaps up its terms, and the commentators sort them. Clarke distinguishes the iniquities, which are transgressions of the law and exposed the man to the most grievous punishment, from the sins, his innumerable deviations from the strict rule of truth and righteousness; the one forgiven, the other entirely removed out of sight and thrown into oblivion. Ellicott puts the stress on the first word: the sins are not abolished but forgiven, not annihilated but covered up, removed from sight, hidden by the absolving grace of God. Barnes is careful that covered here has no reference to the atonement but simply to hiding or concealing, and quotes Calvin's summary that justification with Paul is nothing else but pardon of sin. Gill fills in what became of them: they were imputed to the Son as surety, who bore them and took them away, so that those he justifies now appear before the throne without fault, and will never be charged with them again.
9:
Gill notes that the word only is supplied by the translators, though he defends it: it stands in the Claromontane exemplar used by Beza and in the Vulgate and Ethiopic versions, and the sense requires it. Clarke calls the question a nervous one. If this pardon is essential to happiness, and David says it is, is it then the exclusive privilege of the Jews? It cannot be; for since it comes by the mere mercy of God through faith, the circumcision cannot so much as claim it, and if God offers it to them not for obedience but of mercy, the same blessedness may be offered to the Gentiles who believe. Barnes sets out the remaining inquiry with precision: Abraham's justification by faith is granted, and the only question left is whether it fell after his circumcision or before. If after, a Jew might still plead that even the faith was acceptable because the man was circumcised; if before, the plea collapses, and the father of the nation stands as a man reckoned God's friend while in the very condition the heathen world was then in.

Calvin will not let the argument be narrowed to a rite. Some conclude unwisely, he says, that because circumcision and uncircumcision alone are named the question is only about ceremonies; but we ought to consider what sort of men Paul was reasoning with. The Jews gloried in circumcision not as the symbol of God's favour but as a meritorious observance of the law, and on that account reckoned themselves better than others. It is mentioned here as the initial work, the basis of the righteousness of the law, so that under one thing is included every work to which reward can be due. His reasoning then rests on the order of causes and effects, since the cause is always before its effect: if Abraham's righteousness was the remission of sins, and he attained it before circumcision, remission is not given for preceding merits. Ellicott makes the same shape plainer by taking the sentence out of its interrogative form — the blessedness belongs to the uncircumcised as well, and here is the premise that proves it.

The premise is a matter of dates, and Clarke counts them out. Faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness at least a year before Ishmael was born; he was eighty-six at that birth, and ninety-nine when circumcision was instituted, with Ishmael then thirteen — some fourteen or fifteen years after the reckoning. Wesley states it in one line: not after he was circumcised, for he was justified before Ishmael was born. Henry allows the wider estimate, fourteen years or by some accounts twenty-five, and draws out what the interval is for. Abraham was pardoned and accepted in uncircumcision, a circumstance which might at once silence the fears of the poor uncircumcised Gentiles and lower the pride and conceitedness of the Jews, who gloried in their circumcision as if they had the monopoly of all happiness. Robertson adds that this was a pertinent point the average Jew had not noticed.
11:
Barnes takes the two words apart. A sign is that by which something is shown or represented, and circumcision publicly showed the relation Abraham stood in to God; a seal is the mark of wax attached to a deed to confirm it, or the device stamped from a signet often worn as a ring on the finger, and to affix it was to ratify an engagement already made. Circumcision is called a seal in that sense: a public attestation to the fact that God had previously approved of Abraham and made him promises. Robertson notes the grammar is a genitive of apposition — circumcision being the sign — and presses the consequence: the rite did not convey the righteousness but only gave outward confirmation to a faith already held in uncircumcision. Ellicott says the same against the contemporary view: circumcision was not the cause or condition of Israel's privileges so much as the ratification of a state of things already existing, so that for those who inherited that state the want of the rite was no bar. Wesley reads the seal simply as an assurance on God's part that he accounted the man righteous upon his believing.

What the rite positively signified is disputed. Gill ties it narrowly to the peculiar covenant God made with Abraham and his natural seed concerning Canaan, a distinctive badge marking that posterity off from other peoples, and denies at length that it was a type of baptism: circumcision was confined to males and to Abraham's natural seed, it bears no resemblance to the supposed antitype, and it plainly did not cease when baptism came in but continued in force until the death of Christ. Clarke goes the other way, gathering the constant Jewish usage of the words for mark and seal for the cutting in the flesh, and holding with Taylor that the covenant of the seventeenth chapter of Genesis sealed no new grant but the justification and promise already received. Calvin uses the verse for sacraments in general: they are seals by which the promises of God are in a manner imprinted on our hearts, dead and unprofitable symbols to the reprobate, yet never losing their import, for our unbelief cannot weaken or extinguish the truth of God.

The fatherhood then runs in two directions, and the order matters. Clarke observes that the covenant was made with Abraham while he was still a Gentile, so that the Gentiles were primarily included in it and the Jews brought in consequentially — an unanswerable conclusion, he thinks, and one that must confound the Jews on this point for ever. Ellicott states the reverse guard: the mere performance of the rite was no guarantee of justification unless attended by a faith like Abraham's, and of the two things faith alone was essential, the sign useless without it. Calvin turns this on the schoolmen, who deny justifying power to the older sacraments and assign it to the newer: if Paul reasons correctly that circumcision does not justify because Abraham was justified by faith, the same reason holds against baptism. Cyril, preaching to catechumens, keeps to the pattern — Abraham did many things well, but was never called the friend of God except when he believed, and through faith he left parents, country, and home.
13:
Nobody can point to the phrase heir of the world in Genesis, and Barnes says so plainly: the expression is not found in the promises made to Abraham, and Paul is summing up in one comprehensive title everything that was promised him — a great nation, a blessing on all the families of the earth, a posterity numbering as the stars, a father of many nations. Robertson agrees the promise is not one text but the whole chain, and observes that in these verses Paul takes the keywords of his gospel, faith and promise and grace, and arrays them against the current Jewish theology of law and works and merit. Gill canvasses the narrower readings and rejects them. It cannot simply mean the Gentiles, since the promise is made to Abraham's seed as well as to himself, and believers cannot be both the heirs and the inheritance; nor can it be the land of Canaan by a figure of the part for the whole, since that land is never so called, and the promise of it belonged to those under the law. Ellicott notes the Jews themselves explained the promise of the universal sovereignty of the Messiah.

The point of naming it here, though, is chronological. Henry observes that the promise was made long before the law, and that it points at Christ, being the word that in Abraham all families of the earth should be blessed. What the law does is work wrath, by showing that every transgressor is exposed to the divine displeasure; so God appointed the title to the promised blessings to run by faith, that it might be wholly of grace and made sure to all who are of the like precious faith with Abraham, Jew or Gentile, in every age. Barnes stresses that the covenant preceded both the law of circumcision and the law of Moses and was independent of both. Calvin says the two are now set squarely against each other, and that this ought to be carefully observed: if faith borrows nothing from the law in order to justify, then it has respect to nothing whatever except the mercy of God. He disposes of the reading that limits this to ceremonies with a grammarian's point — had works contributed anything, the text should have said through the law of nature rather than through the written law.

What the heir actually inherits is drawn wide. Calvin takes the inheritance to be eternal life, the country above, of which Canaan was a type and a pledge; and since the fallen state of the whole world was also to be repaired through Christ, the dominion of the world was rightly promised, some taste of which the godly have even now, partaking with a peaceable conscience of what God has made. He adds that consciences enjoy solid peace only when they know that what is not justly due to them is freely given. Clarke reads the title as office: Abraham is the medium through whom the mercy of God is communicated to the world, and the manner of his justification is the rule according to which all men may expect the same blessing, so that every person may now claim justification through faith in virtue of that original grant. Wesley makes the heirship shared — Christ is heir of the world and of all things, and so are all Abraham's seed. Ellicott marks the three stages the verse assumes: faith, then imputed righteousness, then access to the Messianic kingdom with all its privileges.
14:
The argument turns on a consequence nobody would accept. Barnes spells it out: if those who seek acceptance by the law are the heirs, then faith has no place in the scheme at all, and the strong commendation bestowed on Abraham's faith was bestowed without any just cause. A promise looks to the future, and its whole design is to excite trust in the one who makes it; so men who are justified by conformity to Moses cannot be depending on any promise made to Abraham — they have cut themselves off from it and stand independent of it. This is as true now, Barnes adds, of men who seek to be justified by their morality or their forms of religion: they stand outside any promise God has made, on a scheme of their own devising, one that would render the atonement of Christ and the work of the Spirit of no value. Robertson notes the two perfect passives, faith emptied of all meaning and the promise made permanently idle. Ellicott renders the first the same way — emptied of its meaning, become an empty name — and observes there is nothing left for either faith or promise to do if the votaries of law as such are to inherit the kingdom. Clarke calls faith on that supposition entirely useless.

Calvin argues it as an impossibility, and the impossibility is pastoral. Had God attached the condition that he would favour with adoption only those who deserved it, or who performed the law, no one could ever have dared to feel confident that the inheritance belonged to him; for who is so conscious of perfection as to feel assured it is his due? Such a condition would not merely hold men's minds in suspense and anxiety but fill them with fear and trembling, and the promises, which avail nothing except as they are received with full assurance, would be voided in the receiving. Consciences would have no certainty, would be harassed with perpetual inquietude, and at length sink in despair. From this Calvin draws his account of what faith is: not a naked knowledge of God or of his truth, nor a simple persuasion that God is and that his word is true, but a sure knowledge of God's mercy received from the gospel, which brings peace of conscience toward God and rest to the mind. Wesley notes the condition the argument assumes, of those who have kept the whole law.

The reason follows in the next verse, and it is the law's own effect. Gill insists the wrath meant is not man's but God's: the law is so far from justifying sinners that it curses and condemns them, and when it is let into the conscience it fills a man with terrible apprehensions and a fearful looking for of judgment. Calvin allows that it can show the good and the perfect the way of life, but as it prescribes to the sinful what they ought to do and supplies no power for doing it, it only exhibits them as guilty before the tribunal of God; and he rejects as ingenious but unsuitable the reading that makes the wrath the sinner's own, kindled against a Lawgiver opposed to his lusts. Barnes takes the maxim as common justice and common sense — a law expresses what may and may not be done, and where no such rule is given there can be no crime — and turns it against the objector: the more just and reasonable the law, the less hope of being justified by it. Robertson puts it in a line: there is no responsibility for the violation of a non-existent law.
16:
Faith and grace answer to each other, and the commentators labour the correspondence. Barnes puts it simply: the plan is by faith so that it may be a matter of mere undeserved mercy, since if men were justified by law it would be by their own merits. Gill guards the same point from the other side — faith is not the cause or condition of the blessing but the appointed means of receiving it, and since faith is itself a gift of God's grace and consists purely in taking favours at his hand and giving him all the glory of them, everything received by faith is manifestly by grace. Ellicott draws the consequence for scope: faith on man's part is correlative with grace on God's, and salvation, being dependent on grace, is as wide and universal as grace itself and knows no restriction of law. Clarke quotes Taylor to the same effect, that the two mutually infer each other — if a blessing is God's gift we must be persuaded of the goodness that bestows it, and if faith in that goodness is the principle of our hope then the blessing is not due in strict justice; grace, being the mere good will of the donor, is free and open to all whom he chooses.

That is what makes the promise sure. Barnes observes that had it depended on entire conformity to the law it would never have been established at all, since none would ever have yielded such obedience; Robertson glosses the adjective as stable, fast, firm. Calvin treats the verse as the winding up of the whole argument and states it as a syllogism: if the heirship of salvation comes to us by works, faith in it vanishes and the promise is abolished; but both must be sure and certain; hence it comes by faith, so that its stability, being based on the goodness of God alone, is secured. He notes what this implies about faith itself — the Apostle regards it as a thing firm and certain, and so counts hesitancy and doubt as unbelief, whereas the schoolmen dignify that same doubting as a moral conjecture and put it in faith's place. And grace here cannot mean the gift of regeneration, since regeneration is never perfect in this life and could never suffice to pacify a soul or make a promise certain.

The last clause opens the door. Calvin takes those of the law to mean simply the Jewish nation to whom the law was delivered, and argues that the Gentiles were made Abraham's seed by the very oracle that conferred the heirship, since he was made the father not of one nation but of many; the past tense of that word marks the certainty of the divine counsel, for though nothing was then less apparent, God had so decreed. He adds that the fatherhood in view is spiritual, held not from Abraham's flesh but from the promise of God, lest the Jews glory too much in carnal descent. Ellicott says the promise reaches beyond that part of the race which belongs to the dispensation of the Law to those descended from Abraham in a spiritual sense by imitating his faith. Clarke reasons in both directions: of the Gentiles there can be no doubt, since the promise was given while Abraham was himself a Gentile, and the Jews may be inferred, since they sprang from him after he became heir of the righteousness which is received by faith. Wesley makes the condition explicit — Gentiles also, if they follow his faith.
17:
The proof text is the naming scene in Genesis, and Clarke sets it in its covenant frame: the words come with the change from Abram to Abraham, and constitute him head of many nations, the Gentile world, by virtue of the covenant then made. Barnes notices what Paul is leaning on. The Hebrew verb means to give or grant, and also to set or constitute, and the tense is past — I have made thee — so that God speaks of a thing as already done which he had only purposed; in his own mind he had so constituted him, and the fulfilment was so certain that it could be spoken of as accomplished. Gill takes the plural as decisive against a merely national reading, since the Jews cannot be called many nations, and concludes the fatherhood must be understood in a spiritual sense; Robertson says the same in a phrase, that it is true only of spiritual children, of Abraham as father of those who believe God.

The next words place him somewhere. Ellicott would render them in the presence of rather than before, and connects them closely with the clause the parenthesis interrupts: Abraham stands as the father of us all in the presence of that God in whom he believed, confronting the Almighty as he had done when the promise was first given him. Robertson notes the preposition means right in front of, and that Paul has drawn the antecedent into the relative clause. Wesley points out how much rests on that presence, since before men nothing of this appeared, those nations being then unborn. Henry allows both readings and finds each true: Abraham became the father of many nations before him whom he believed, that is, in the eye and account of God — or else like him whom he believed, for as God was a common Father, so was Abraham.

Then come the two titles, and Henry observes that faith fastens on God himself, other foundation being what no man can lay; it is the holy wisdom and policy of faith to fasten particularly on that in God which is accommodated to the difficulties it has to wrestle with. Abraham, promised a son when he and Sarah were as good as dead, looks on God as one who could breathe life into dry bones. Barnes reads the first title the same way, as answering the strong natural improbability of the case. Calvin makes the pivot: a seed was promised to Abraham as though he were in vigour and strength, and he was as it were dead, so he had to raise his thoughts to the power by which the dead are quickened — and it is therefore not strange that the Gentiles, barren and dead, should be brought into the same society, so that whoever denies them capable of grace does wrong to Abraham. He turns it into a pattern of every calling: when we are called by the Lord we emerge from nothing, and to be in a suitable state to hear that call we must be altogether dead in ourselves. Wesley illustrates the second title by the difference between two commands — a man says to a servant already existing, Do this, and he does it, but God says to the light while it does not exist, Go forth, and it goes.
18:
Robertson calls the opening phrase a graphic picture — past hope, upon hope, he trusted. Calvin explains why the one word can stand on both sides of the clause: in the first instance it means a probable evidence for hoping, such as may be derived from nature and carnal reason; in the second it means the hope given by God. He notes an alternative rendering, above hope, and half prefers it, since unless faith flies upward on celestial wings so as to look down on all the perceptions of the flesh as on things far below, it will stick fast in the mud of the world. Nothing, he adds, is more injurious to faith than to fasten our minds to our eyes, seeking from what we see a reason for our hope. Ellicott points out a shift easily missed: the relative here refers to Abraham, where in the previous verse it referred to God, and the force of the preposition is that he grounded his faith upon hope — an internal hope strong within him though there were no objective grounds for hoping at all. Wesley distinguishes the two organs on the same object: the promise is apprehended by faith as a thing which God has spoken, and by hope as a good thing which God has promised to us.

Clarke sets the improbabilities in a row, since the strength of the faith is measured by them. Abraham had as yet no child by Sarah; he was a hundred years old and she ninety; and beyond the unlikelihood of her bearing at that age, she had been barren all her life. Every one of these was a reason not to credit the promise, and the promise itself was large, that in his posterity all the nations of the earth should be blessed. Clarke reduces the whole to two clauses — God cannot lie; Abraham can believe. Barnes makes the same point as a rule: faith looks to the strength of God, not to second causes or to the difficulties that appear formidable to men. Gill observes that neither the length of time since the promise was made nor the seemingly insuperable difficulties of nature weakened it. Robertson notices that the qualifying word about softens the exactness of the numeral, the first promise of a son having come when Abraham was eighty-six and the second when he was ninety-nine, calling himself a hundred.

Whether he looked at the difficulty or looked away from it is disputed, and the dispute is textual. Ellicott holds that on the evidence of the best manuscripts the negative should be dropped, so that the sense runs: because he was not weak in faith he considered indeed — took full account of — the natural impediments to the promise, and yet did not doubt. Calvin keeps the negative and reads it as a deliberate withdrawal: Abraham turned his mind from what met his own eyes and as it were forgot himself, though we are not to think he had no regard whatever to his body, since Scripture records him asking whether a child should be born to a man of a hundred years. It was the greater effort, Calvin thinks, to lay the consideration aside than never to have entertained it. He will not follow Augustine, who put the impediment in Sarah alone, since the man who was before like a dry and barren tree was afterwards so invigorated by the blessing that he begot other children still — which makes the divine power more visible rather than less. And he distinguishes two weaknesses of faith, the one that succumbs to adversity and falls away, the other that arises from imperfection and does not extinguish faith at all, so that the faithful may be said to be strong even in their weakness.
20:
Robertson takes the verb apart: it means to separate, to distinguish between, to decide between, and in this passive sense to be divided in one's own mind — Abraham was not divided in his mind by unbelief — while the answering verb means to have power put into one. Calvin renders it as an inquiry rather than a hesitation, and defends the choice: Abraham did not try to find out, by weighing the matter in the balance of unbelief, whether the Lord was able to perform what he had promised, since to search a thing out is properly to examine it through mistrust. Ellicott would translate the second clause through faith rather than in faith, to answer the through unbelief before it — unbelief did not make him doubt, but faith made him confident and strong. Gill turns the negative into a general rule: there is no reason to stagger at any promise of God, since the promises are made by one who cannot lie, his faithfulness is engaged to perform them, every promise is in Christ yea and amen, and never yet did one of them fail.

But Abraham did ask how it could come to pass, and Calvin will not pretend otherwise. That was the asking of a man astonished, as it was with the virgin Mary when she inquired of the angel; saints who hear of works exceeding their comprehension burst out in wonder, but pass quickly on to lay hold of the power of God, whereas the wicked examine the message and scoff at it as a fable. So Abraham was not reproved for laughing and asking whether a child could be born to a man of a hundred, for in his astonishment he fully admitted the power of God's word, while Sarah's like laughter was reproved, because she did not regard the promise as valid. The clause about glory then follows naturally. Barnes reads it as honour paid by firmness: those who believe God's promises bear testimony that he is worthy of confidence, becoming so many witnesses that God has a claim upon the trust of mankind. Ellicott notes the phrase need not mean any verbal ascription of praise, but covers whatever tends to God's glory in thought, word, or deed, and here means the frank recognition of his omnipotence. Calvin puts it at the root: no greater honour can be given to God than by faith to seal his truth, and true religion begins there.

The last clause states what was actually believed. Robertson glosses the participle as bearing full measure or settling fully, a late word common in the papyri for finishing off or paying off a debt; Clarke says the man's soul was full of confidence that the truth of God bound him to fulfil his promise and his power enabled him to do it. Barnes observes this was not the only occasion, since the same implicit confidence appeared when Abraham was commanded to sacrifice the promised son. Calvin thinks the statement looks slight and is not, for all men acknowledge God's power in the abstract while nothing is more uncommon than to ascribe to it the honour it deserves. When there is no contest nobody denies that God can do all things; as soon as an obstacle impedes the course of a promise, we cast his power down from its eminence, and excuse ourselves by saying the defect we feel is in us and not in him. But we do not sufficiently exalt that power unless we think it greater than our own weakness; and faith does not merely grant that God can do all things while leaving him sitting still, but regards his power as in continual exercise, ready to execute whatever he has declared by his mouth.
22:
Gill asks what in Abraham's faith earned the reckoning, and answers that nothing did: it was imputed not because his faith was strong or because he had a full assurance of it, but because it was right, resting on the promise of God and relying on his power and faithfulness to perform it. He draws out the consequence at once — the righteousness of faith is imputed to all who have true faith though it be weak, since faith is the same in all true believers as to nature, kind, and object, and differs only in degree. Barnes reads the verse as a verdict: the faith was so implicit that it demonstrated Abraham was the firm friend of God, and he was treated accordingly. Clarke follows Taylor's paraphrase, that God was graciously pleased to place the man's faith to his account and to allow his reliance upon the divine goodness and power to stand as a title to a blessing which, having been an idolater, he otherwise had no right to. He insists on the pronoun: the text does not say that any righteousness, his own or another's, was reckoned to him, but that it — his faith — was. Calvin ties the whole to the word: faith can bring us nothing more than what it receives from the word, and a man is not made just by being imbued with a general and confused idea that God is true, unless he reposes on the promise of his favour.

Then the record turns outward. Henry denies that the sentence was meant for an historical commendation of Abraham or a report of something peculiar to him; the accounts of the Old Testament saints were never intended as histories merely, to inform and divert us, but as precedents to direct us — written for us that are mean and vile, who come so far short of Abraham in privileges and performances, and for Gentiles as well as Jews, since the grace of God is the same yesterday, today, and for ever. Barnes states the same in a sentence: God has but one mode of justifying men, so if Abraham was regarded and treated as righteous, then on that same principle all others may be. Clarke says the fact was not recorded as a mere circumstance in the patriarch's life, and Wesley that it was not set down to do personal honour to him.

Calvin knows the logical weakness of the move and says so: a proof from example is not always valid, which is precisely why Paul expressly affirms that what was exhibited in Abraham was a common righteousness belonging equally to all. He grants the heathen maxim that history is the teacher of what life ought to be, but denies that anyone can draw sound instruction from history as they hand it down; Scripture alone justly claims that office, prescribing the rules by which every other history may be tested. Its own uses he numbers three — to frame our life by the patience of the saints, to confirm faith by the help God gave them in adversity, and to stir us up by his judgments on the wicked. Chrysostom anticipates the reader who asks what this is to us, since it was Abraham who was justified, and answers that Paul places us close to the Patriarch again: a Gentile lately come near, who has done no work, is in nothing inferior to the believing Jew, nor even to the Patriarch, but rather greater, for Abraham's faith is but the type of ours. And Paul does not argue that if it was reckoned to him it will probably be reckoned to us, lest he make the matter a syllogism; he speaks in the authentic words of Scripture. Robertson notes the conjunction may be recitative or declarative, and makes sense either way.
24:
The pronoun that Clarke pressed two verses back now divides the bench. Gill holds that what was reckoned to Abraham was not his faith but the righteousness which his faith looked to and laid hold on, and argues from the transfer itself: Abraham's faith could never be reckoned for righteousness to another, nor indeed was it so reckoned to him, yet those who believe as he did have the very same righteousness imputed to them that he had. Clarke keeps the case as he stated it, that faith was accepted in the place of an obedience the man could not bring, and reads the record as the model according to which God will save both Jews and Gentiles — there being no other way, since all have sinned; and if God wills our salvation it must be by faith, for faith contemplates his promise, and his promise comprehends the Son of his love. Barnes settles the continuity on a different footing. Faith is belief in God just so far as he has revealed his will to us, and so is the same in principle though its objects differ: Abraham's leading truth was a numerous posterity, ours is that God gave his Son to die and raised him up and is ready through him to pardon, so that the faith of Abraham and of all believers is substantially one thing, varied only by what has been made known.

The clause identifies God by an act. Ellicott thinks an association of ideas has led Paul here, since the birth of Isaac resembles the resurrection of Christ in that both involved the exercise of omnipotence — the omnipotence Abraham believed and we are to believe — and adds that the Apostle is drawn to mention it because of the place the Resurrection held in his gospel; Robertson simply notes that the fact of it is central for Paul. Wesley draws the consequence for the object of trust: God the Father is therefore the proper object of justifying faith, and he observes that Paul, describing both our faith and Abraham's, puts a part for the whole, choosing in Abraham's case the part that would most affect Jewish readers. He also uses the verse against those who reduce the terms to labels, making justification by works mean by Judaism and justification by faith mean by embracing Christianity; on that reading Abraham could be justified in neither way, and David would have been justified by works and not by faith.

Calvin explains why the periphrasis is worth the space. Had Paul said only that we believe in God, it could not so readily have been learnt how believing serves to obtain righteousness; but when Christ comes forth and presents in his own resurrection a sure pledge of life, it appears plainly from what fountain the imputation of righteousness flows, since the resurrection is no small part of faith and is the ground of our hope as to eternal life. Cyril, preaching on the same article, turns it into an exhortation and a warning: since we have the prophecies, let faith abide with us, and let those fall who fall through unbelief, for you have taken your stand on the rock of the faith in the Resurrection. He names the danger of his own day, the Manichees who still say the Saviour's rising was phantom-wise and not real, and who do not heed the Apostle's own words about the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead. Gill closes the circle where Paul opened it, that the faith is truly of the same kind, since Abraham too believed in God who quickens the dead.
25:
Gill traces the handing over through every set of hands: Christ was delivered by Judas to the chief priests, by them to Pilate, by Pilate to the Jews and the Roman soldiers, and by his Father into the hands of justice and death according to his determinate counsel — yet not without his own free consent, who voluntarily laid down his life and gave himself a ransom. He then narrows the beneficiaries as deliberately as he widened the agents. Christ was delivered for no offences of his own, since he committed none; nor for those of angels, for these were not spared; nor for those of all men, since all will not be saved; but for the offences of God's elect. Ellicott glosses delivered as delivered to death, and reads the preposition as because of — that is, in order that he might atone for them. Wesley states it in three words, as an atonement for them.

Calvin holds that the two prepositions in the verse, spelled the same, do not mean the same: the first gives the why, the second the end for which. He knows the first is sometimes emptied out by those who render it merely on account of, in order to evade the idea of a propitiation, and answers from the rest of Scripture — the ransom sayings, the declaration that Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many, and John's word for expiation. It cannot then mean anything but that God delivered his Son as a sacrifice for our offences. Clarke agrees about the atonement, heaping up the texts on redemption through his blood, but dissents on what is imputed. The doctrine of the imputed righteousness of Christ as held by many, he says, will not readily be found in this chapter where it has been supposed to stand in all its proofs; it is repeatedly said that faith is imputed for righteousness, and nowhere here that Christ's obedience to the moral law is imputed to any man. The law once broken no longer required obedience but death, so redemption comes by the merit of his passion, not by his law-keeping in our stead — a much higher price. And since the law can claim only the death of a transgressor, Clarke thinks it the greatest miracle of all that Christ could die at all, whose life was never forfeited.

How the rising bears on justification is the last question, and Ellicott answers it by rank: the death is the proper cause, the resurrection only the mediate or secondary cause, for the atoning efficacy lay in the death while the proof of that efficacy was the Resurrection, which gave the greatest impulse to faith in the cross and in that way helped bring justification about. Barnes gives three reasons rather than a ranking. The rising completed the work, since a sacrifice that did not conquer death would have left it imperfect; it proved the work accepted by the Father; and it is the mainspring of all our hope, there being no satisfactory evidence that man can be raised at all except that Christ was. Calvin divides the same ground: our sins were expiated by the death, and by the resurrection our righteousness was obtained, the beginning of righteousness being reconciliation with God and its completion the attaining of life by the abolishing of death. He adds a note on the passive — Paul says delivered rather than died, because the expiation depended on the eternal goodwill of God, who purposed to be in this way pacified. Robertson enters the caution the whole bench would accept, that Paul does not mean to separate the resurrection from the death in the work of atonement, but to show that the two stand at one in proof of Christ's claims.
